chapters.title: Chapter 2: The Life of an ESOP

lessons.title: Vesting Schedules and Cliffs: When Your Options Become Yours

children.text: Two candidates get offers from the same company on the same day. Both letters say 4,800 options at an exercise price of ₹20. One of them will walk away with lakhs more than the other, and the reason is buried in a single line neither of them read closely: the vesting schedule.
A
vesting schedule
is not a formality. It decides how much of your grant is real on any given day, and almost nobody leaves a company exactly on a vesting anniversary.

markDefs.definition: The timetable that decides how many of your granted options you have earned at any given date.

body.text: Your grant size tells you what you could earn if you stay to the very end. Your vesting schedule tells you what you actually have on the day you leave. Only the second number is ever real.

children.text: The Indian Default, and Why It Exists

The standard Indian startup schedule is four years with a one-year cliff: nothing for twelve months, 25% in one step at the first anniversary, and the remaining 75% in monthly or quarterly instalments over the next three years. Large listed companies more often use equal annual tranches. Both satisfy the legal minimum of one year between grant and vesting.

body.label: Indian startups granting ESOPs to every employee
body.context: Qapita survey data for 2024, up from roughly one in four in 2021. ESOPs have moved from a leadership perk towards a company-wide one.

children.text: Same Grant, Three Schedules, Very Different Money

Take one grant of 4,800 options and run it through three schedules. Schedule A is the startup default: a one-year cliff of 1,200 options, then 100 options a month. Schedule B vests 25% on each anniversary. Schedule C is back-loaded at 10%, 20%, 30% and 40% a year.

body.title: Cumulative options vested under three schedules

children.text: At the four-year mark all three arrive at the same place. That is exactly why grant letters look identical at first glance. The difference shows up everywhere in between.
The month-30 exit
Say you resign two and a half years in, at month 30, with an exercise price of ₹20 and a fair market value of ₹320 per share.

body.caption: Vested options and pre-tax value on a month-30 exit

stats.label: Schedule B
stats.context: 2,400 vested, since month 30 falls between anniversaries

stats.label: Schedule C
stats.context: Only 1,440 vested, because most value sits in year four

children.text: Identical offer letters, identical exercise price, identical resignation date, and a gap of ₹4,68,000 between the best and worst outcome.
The schedule is the offer.

body.title: Count the Forfeited Options
body.prompt: Under back-loaded Schedule C (10%, 20%, 30% and 40% vesting annually on a 4,800-option grant), how many options does an employee forfeit by resigning at month 30?
body.explanation: By month 30 only years one and two have completed, so 10% + 20% = 30% of 4,800 has vested, which is 1,440 options. The remaining 3,360 options, worth ₹10,08,000 at this valuation, go back to the company.

children.text: Cliffs: The Most Expensive Date in Your Calendar
A
cliff

turns vesting into a step function. One year of work produces nothing on day 364 and 25% on day 366. Cliffs exist to filter out early exits and bad hires, and they do that job well. They also produce genuinely brutal outcomes for people who leave, or are asked to leave, just before the date.

markDefs.definition: An initial period during which nothing vests. Cross it and the first block vests in one step; leave before it and you get nothing.

body.text: If you are resigning, being let go, or negotiating an exit within a few weeks of your cliff, say so and ask to move the last working day past it. It is a normal, reasonable request, and the cost to the company is usually far smaller than the value to you.

body.title: The Cliff Question
body.question: Ramesh has a one-year cliff on 1 July. He is offered a new job starting 15 June and negotiates his last working day at his current employer as 30 June. What happens to his options?
options: He vests 25% because he completed eleven and a half months
He vests nothing, since he leaves one day before the cliff
He vests a pro-rated share for the months worked
His options stay live until he exercises them
body.explanation: A cliff is all or nothing, and it runs on the date, not on effort or proportion. One extra day of employment would have vested 25% of his grant. This is the single most common self-inflicted ESOP loss in India.

children.text: Performance and Milestone Vesting: Read the Fine Print
Performance vesting
ties your options to targets rather than to the calendar. It is common for senior hires and sales leaders, and it is entirely reasonable when the target is measurable. The danger is vagueness.

markDefs.definition: Vesting that depends on meeting defined business or individual targets, not only on completing time with the company.

children.text: Good:
options vest if revenue from your business line crosses ₹50 crore in FY 2028, measured from audited financials.
Risky:
options vest on satisfactory performance as determined by the board. You are being granted a discretion, not a right.
Ask:
who measures the target, from which document, and what happens if the company changes strategy and the target becomes irrelevant.

Refresh Grants and the Year Four Problem
Four years in, a fully vested employee has nothing left to lose by leaving. Good companies solve this with
refresh grants

: a new grant made in year two or three, at the exercise price of that day, so some unvested value always sits ahead of you. If you are being retained on ESOPs, ask whether refreshes are part of the plan or a one-time story.

markDefs.definition: A fresh grant made to an existing employee, usually before the original grant is fully vested, so that some unvested value always remains.

children.text: The other question worth asking early is what happens if the company is acquired. Some schemes accelerate vesting, many do not, and the fairest common structure is
double trigger
acceleration. We deal with acquisitions properly later in this chapter.

markDefs.definition: Acceleration that needs two events: the company is acquired, and the employee is terminated or materially demoted soon after.

body.title: Monthly vesting vs annual tranches, from the employee’s side

columns.label: Monthly after the cliff
points: You earn value every single month
Leaving mid-year still keeps most of that year
Easier to plan an exit around
Slightly more administration for the company

columns.label: Annual tranches
points: Value arrives only on anniversary dates
Leaving eleven months in loses the whole year
Creates pressure to stay right up to each date
Simpler to administer and common at large firms

body.title: What to Ask About Vesting Before You Sign
steps: How long is the cliff, and what is the exact date?
After the cliff, does vesting run monthly, quarterly or annually?
Is the schedule equal or back-loaded across the years?
Is any part of it tied to performance, and who measures the target?
Does vesting continue during notice period, long leave or a sabbatical?
Are refresh grants normal here, and at what stage?
Does vesting accelerate if the company is acquired, and is it single or double trigger?

body.title: Designing a Schedule That Actually Retains People
body.scenario: Priyanka founded a 45-person logistics SaaS company in Ahmedabad. Her last two senior hires left at months 26 and 31, both forfeiting large unvested balances under a back-loaded 10/20/30/40 schedule. Her investors like the retention effect. Her recruiters say candidates now negotiate hard on vesting and two have walked away.
body.prompt: Should she change the schedule, and what would you advise?
body.modelAnswer: The back-loaded schedule is punishing exits rather than preventing them. People left anyway, so the company got the reputational cost without the retention benefit. A sensible move is to shift new grants to the market standard of four years with a one-year cliff and monthly vesting after it, which candidates recognise and trust, and then use refresh grants in year two or three to keep unvested value permanently ahead of senior staff. That spreads retention across time instead of concentrating it in one painful year-four date. She should also review the exercise window, since a short post-exit window can destroy value even for people who vested properly. If investors want a stronger retention lever for the leadership team specifically, performance vesting on clearly measurable targets is a better tool than back-loading everyone.

points: The vesting schedule, not the grant size, decides what you own on the day you leave.
The Indian default is four years with a one-year cliff, then monthly or quarterly vesting.
The same 4,800-option grant was worth ₹9,00,000, ₹7,20,000 or ₹4,32,000 on an identical month-30 exit, purely because of the schedule.
Back-loaded schedules concentrate value in the final year and punish mid-term exits hardest.
A cliff is a date, not a proportion. Leaving days before it means leaving with nothing.
Performance vesting is fine when the target is measurable and documented, and risky when it rests on discretion.
Refresh grants keep unvested value ahead of you and are the real answer to the year-four retention problem.

body.text: This lesson is for education only and is not investment, tax or legal advice. All schedules and figures here are illustrative. Your own scheme document and grant letter govern what you actually hold.
